prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and its active form, which established the physiological basis for GLP-1-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings place B017 first, but unanimity is not the argument. On the evidence, GLP-1 is one of the few cases where a physiological discovery (gut hormone, glucose-dependent insulin secretion, central appetite effects) runs unbroken into a drug class with large randomized outcome data in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal endpoints. The discovery is original, independently confirmed over decades, and clearly mature. I would frame the prize around the hormone and its active peptide form, because that is the discovery that makes the later pharmacology possible.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Four credited names compete for three places, the priority question over who first defined the active GLP-1(7-36) form is contested, and the supplied list omits other early investigators. Rewarding physiology alone risks excluding the drug-development step that actually produced liraglutide and semaglutide, which is what changed clinical practice. A prize that is seen as unfair in its credit would weaken an otherwise very strong scientific case.

responses.point: Proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen for B017, arguing that the pairing of basic physiology with the design of long-acting agonists best matches the clinical impact.
responses.response: I take this seriously and it is the main fork between us. I still prefer Mojsov over Knudsen because the prize is strongest when it rewards the discovery of the hormone and its bioactive form, and drug optimisation by an industrial team is more naturally covered by other recognition. I accept that your configuration better captures why the therapies exist, and I would not call mine clearly superior. The point turns on whether the committee wants to reward discovery or development, and your own opening lists the Mojsov dispute as unresolved from recollection rather than verified.

responses.point: Supports Drucker, Holst and Knudsen and raises the question of whether the committee prefers recognising physiology or drug development, noting that Habener and others may have claims.
responses.response: I share your concern about a three-way split being contested, and I agree that Habener-type claims cannot be settled from the supplied record. Where I differ is that omitting Knudsen leaves out the long-acting analogues, so I accept that a purely physiological citation understates the clinical chain. I would keep the citation worded around the hormone and its active form so that the omission is a principled choice and not an oversight.

responses.point: Considers Drucker, Holst and Mojsov the most defensible scientific trio, with Knudsen's contribution mainly pharmaceutical, and ranks B024 imatinib third.
responses.response: I agree with the trio and with the reading that the physiology is the defensible core. On B024, I agree it is very mature and conceptually foundational, but I see it as a drug-development prize whose upstream BCR-ABL and Philadelphia chromosome discoveries lie outside the credited names. That makes it a weaker second option than B006 for me, though I would keep it as an alternative.

responses.point: Ranks B017 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and notes that appetite effects in the central nervous system add a neuroendocrine appeal, while placing B024 second and B016 third.
responses.response: I agree on the trio. I would give the central appetite effects less weight than you do, since the case rests on the peripheral incretin physiology and the outcome data, and the CNS mechanism is still being worked out. I also disagree gently on B016. The HPV VLP case has real public health weight, but the Frazer and Zhou priority dispute and the overlap with the 2008 prize make its attribution riskier than B017 or B006.

responses.point: Includes only June and Sadelain for B006, treating Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer as a distinct contribution, and notes that Eshhar's original chimeric receptor concept is outside the supplied names.
responses.response: Your two-person B006 is a fair correction to my opening three-person list, where I included Rosenberg too readily. If B006 comes forward as my alternative, I would support June and Sadelain unless the committee decides adoptive cell transfer is a separate discovery. The Eshhar gap remains and I cannot resolve it from the supplied names.

uncertainties: Whether the committee rewards the discovery of the hormone and its active form, or also the drug-development step represented by Knudsen.
Priority for identification of the active GLP-1 peptide among Mojsov, Habener and others, which I have not independently verified.
Whether any other shortlisted discovery would be better paired with B017 as a second prize part, or whether a single achievement is cleaner.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B017 or the alternatives from the provided profile. My documented ties (Grillner, Ernfors, a 2009 paper with Perlmann) concern motor circuits and stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons, not the shortlisted candidates. The shortlisted optogenetics candidate B049 touches my field but I do not propose it.
